w:r.w:t: DM i Tetris 2025 - Game Boy Tetris Qual ROM
In April 2025, I was approached by Pernille from the Danish Community about a ROM hack they wanted to use for qualification for the upcoming Danish championships.

At this point I was already very familiar with ROM patching and had done quite a lot of projects. This one actually came at the perfect time, because I had some time to do it and it was the perfect reason for me to actually work on a bare bone version of Tetris to be used for future projects.
So, it was a no brainer for me to
do it. So, as I heard a Tetris person say before
– overdeliver.” I agreed to have a look.
Immediately I started coming up with tons of ideas to give it a very personal touch for the Danes and their event. A lot of blood, sweat and tears went into the event, so I didn’t want to disappoint.
Given the original message I could start with this:
“A-Type game with a countdown of 5 minutes that force-ends after that.”
The first thing I did was to draw the simplest

So, I lost no time to start with the coding. A first functioning prototype was finished very quickly. But the work only started. Over the next months I crafted the project and optimized code, fixed bugs, improved and most importantly deleted unnecessary code from the codebase bit by bit. New ideas popped up and the final 20% certainly took way more than 80% of the remaining time.
There were some insane bugs and thought experiments I came up with in order to solve certain issues.
This document is mostly based on a document I shared with the organizers. My idea was for them to be able to track progress and give inputs.
The beginning of the document concerns some superficial descriptions and the later part goes in depth (though not too far) how I solved certain issues and what I actually did.

PART II: BUGS, CODE AND HOW STUFF WAS

Note that certain procedures do not fit inside a single frame. It is therefore a good idea to repeat certain calls in a loop (not in the init) where there is a check in place that makes sure the thing is called once. E.g. a variable that starts on $00 and when the procedure is successfully called becomes $01. Then the procedure can be skipped via loading the variable into the accumulator. Using the compare command (CP) then sets the flag register to a certain state (z = zero, nz = non-zero, c = carry, nc = non-carry) that can then be used to conditionally jump (JR or JP) to an upcoming address after the relevant code.
Bug 1: Floor was only partially there (and too low)
This one was a dirty bug and was unexpected. Debugging it was hell.
The conditional end screens “GG Screen” and “Success Screen” are outsourced in binary files and read in as follows:
They are then loaded in 2 steps:
Load tileset into wRAM (comparable to a waiting room), starting at address $C800
From here manipulations (such as adding or removing dancers or musicians) is trivial.
Load the “waiting room” into the BG Map (=Background map, Screen0 in vRAM, starting at address $9800).
This is done row by row in a loop from bottom to top, which creates the curtain animation.

After loading in the game over screen (GG or Success) it loads-in the upcoming values without displaying them. The BG map extends the viewport of the displayed tiles to the right and below. If any of the first couple of rows after a loaded game over screen contains empty cells, these are not recognized as floor tiles for the next game. The problem is, these floor tiles are never displayed anywhere but only their values are stored, which was a nightmare to find the issue because the BG map shows nothing below the playfield and inserting tiles there before the game has no effect.
“GameScreenLayout_GG” contains empty cells in the first rows. These are then not floor tiles in the next game. Therefore, I had to make sure that the “GG” tiles are not loaded after “Success” tiles.

How was I supposed to guess that from studying the invisible floor from the background map below the playfield? Makes you wonder how many times the original developers had no idea what happens to the floor sometimes.

The proper solution would be to add a stop command ($FF) or load at least 1 rows worth of tile IDs that are not $2F (empty tile) after “GameScreenLayout_GG::” and “GameScreenLayout_Success::” (this is a dirty solution!).

The code base of this project is from Vinheim3’s disassembly:

The code might not always perform in the most efficient way, but will certainly do the trick and we have more than enough wiggle room during each frame - I prioritized human-readability over efficiency. The programming is done using
Incrementing (INC) is adding 1 to a number
decrement (DEC) is subtracting 1 from a number
These are extremely basic tasks in assembly.
The Game Boy is an 8-bit system and therefore can store 2^8 (=256) different values on each storage unit (e.g. values at address in ROM, wRAM, vRAM… or the CPU registers a, b, c, d, e, h and l).

Computer logic at its core operates in binary, where 1 bit is either a 0 or 1. To make this more readable, 4 bits are combined to a single digit each: 2^4 = 16 possible values. This requires more numbers than our decimal system can provide. The solution to this is the hexadecimal (hex) system where letters A-F are used to extend the range. The counting goes:
Overflow: During an increment (INC), after reaching F, the the next digit will be affected
Underflow: When decrementing (DEC) and after reaching 0, the previous digit is affected
To distinguish hex from dec values, a prefix is typically used on the hex value (e.g. 0x or $) the same can be done to binary numbers (e.g. 0b or %)
A Byte (256 values) can be displayed using two hex-digits: a high nibble and a low nibble (range from $00 to $FF).
By the way: $0 = %0000 and $F = %1111 (i.e. one nibble consists of 4 bits = half a Byte).
The 2 nibbles of a Byte (high or low) can be extracted by
masking the other nibble via “bitwise AND” ($0F and $F0 respectively)
and in the case of the high nibble, bitwise shifting the result by 4 to the left, which after masking is the same as a “nibble SWAP” ($XY ↔ $YX).

A decimal timer must wrap after 0 (DEC) or 9 (INC). Therefore we need to convert the digits to decimal. BCD is a commonly used concept to achieve this. BCD stands for Binary-Coded Decimal. The two stored nibbles will therefore never contain the hex-exclusive values:
A, B, C, D, E or F.
; Decrement a BCD value in A
; Low nibble is 0, need to borrow from high nibble
Minutes, seconds and frames are stored in a high RAM (hRAM) address each.
These are made up of 1 Byte (2 nibbles) in the BCD format:
“Seconds” and “Frames” range from 0 to 59. “Minutes” at this point only use the lower nibble (0-9).
hResetToMinutes:: ; standard value to reset the timer to
The values for these variables are set during the initialization of the game, in the subroutine “GameState0a_InGameInit:” which is called before a game starts.
ldh a, [hResetToMinutes] ; reset to the chosen minutes value
ldh [hInLastFiveSeconds], a ; last five seconds are not yet reached
ldh [hFlagTimer], a ; flag timer (whenever this reaches x, the flag state is changed)
ldh [hLineClearFrame], a ; we are not in a line clear animation

By the way: “xor a” is a commonly used instruction to set register A (the accumulator) to $00. This replaces the less efficient instruction “ld a, $00”. The same is true for “inc a” after register A contained $00, instead of the less efficient “ld a, $01.”
“wInLastFiveSeconds” and “wTimerOn” are boolean flags ($00 = FALSE, $01 = TRUE).

The countdown has to be called on each frame. The DMG Game Boy operates at ~59.7 FPS (frames per second). In our code, one second is defined as 60 frames, which is accurate enough. This also adds fairness, since the players work with equal amounts of frames across platforms.
I added the countdown logic to ”InGameCheckButtonsPressed:” which is the subroutine that checks for pressed buttons. This subroutine is conveniently called at the start of each frame.

An alternative to setting the background tiles of the timer digits, could be achieved with setting a pointer in hl and then increment (inc hl). I don’t like this method here and it is likely to use more machine cycles anyway.

hRAM is a RAM region and presumably part of the CPU / SoC architecture. Access to these regions (e.g. via “ldh”) is way faster than accessing wRAM for example. It uses fewer machine cycles and only requires 8-bit pointers, instead of the 16-bit pointers (e.g. “ld”) for the other regions, such as wRAM, vRAM or the ROM. Using hRAM for variables that are called often - e.g. on each frame - is very efficient.

The way this is achieved is by loading these screens via binary files into the RAM screen buffer region, located at $C800 (and upcoming) - this acts similar to a waiting room.
From there these tiles are then loaded row-by-row into the background map. This happens together with the curtain animation.

Note that the score is saved (1) in BCD and (2) in the
(LE) format. Little-endian in contrast to big-endian is a way to store bytes in reverse order. It is a very common way to store certain things in assembly and to iterate over the bytes.
A score of 123,456 is therefore stored as: $56, $34, $12 starting at [wScoreBCD]. Just something to note and to be aware of when working with assembly.

In order to add music I needed to make sure there is enough space in ROM and wRAM. The plan was to replace the existing sound engine with a sound engine that is often used nowadays for projects - the “hUGE” sound engine. Since this engine is fundamentally different from the native one, we can’t expect that any of the original music still works. Therefore all music - excluding sound effects - had to be removed as well. This left us with a big chunk of free space in ROM. Since we now removed A LOT of stuff, we could replace certain static address assignments and make them dynamic (= place without a gap to the last code).
Example (static assignment [address $6480 in ROM bank 1] to dynamic assignment)
This allowed it to include the new sound engine.

These files are available online. The hUGE engine is as simple as it gets. There are various DAW (digital audio workstations), such as hUGE tracker or the native GB Studio music player that allows writing music for the Game Boy.

This sound engine also requires enough free wRAM addresses to place the current song to be played. Since due to several cleanups - mostly the unification of the leaderboard - we have more than enough RAM addresses available, I just had to make sure to remove all entries that are no longer needed. Certain buffers could also be removed. This needed to be evaluated carefully to avoid conflicts in double-assigning RAM addresses.
This is an example of a reserved range that might or might not be removed.

I then used the GB Studio music editor to write the music. GB Studio, however, does not allow saving the music files as “.s” or “.asm” files. Therefore I additionally used the “hUGE Tracker” afterwards to open the file from the previously saved folder in the GB Studio project:

The music files are stored as “.uge” files. These can be opened in hUGE tracker and saved as “.asm”. I changed the ending to “.s”, since this fits better the already existing structure. Both would work equally well.
I could then place this file in the file structure of the project alongside the code.

When trying to build the project, it warned me that certain variables in this file were already defined, namely all the variables below that I changed. I added the prefix “d_” to the beginning of each variable.
This of course required changing the variables in the rest of the file. Which was straight forward.
I wonder if there is a way to circumvent this - I guess there must be… this is to be investigated for the next project.

In order to use the music, you only need to initialize the song data. This moves it to wRAM to be used afterwards. The pointer in hl needs to be set to the beginning of the sound file “danish_anthem” (see above).
I added this initialization to the “Gamestate_GameOverInit:”
To play the music, you need to make sure the subroutine “hUGE_dosound” is called on each frame. This plays one frames worth of music and forwards the pointer accordingly.That’s almost all:
I added it - coupled to the necessary conditions - to the very end of “GameState_LevelEndedMain”

It is also recommended to mute or re-enable the channels. For this I created the following subroutines that I call at various transitions. Muted channels will make sure the battery lives longer and will avoid artefacts such as lasting tones.

The anthem was recreated from this video that uses only 2 tones at the same time - perfect for us:
The Game Boy has 3 “tone” channels: duty1, duty2 and wav. I added the 2 tones to duty1 and duty2 and created a new bass line to wav.
The 4th channel is the noise channel that is mostly used to add percussion - this is what I added too. I lowered the percussion volume quite a bit to make it less invasive.
